content.text: The learning rate sets how far each training step moves the weights, not how fast you get the same answer. Too small and training crawls; too big and it bounces around the minimum and stops somewhere worse; far too big and it diverges, sometimes without a single error. Sweep it on a log scale, judge it by the loss, and let a schedule shrink it as training goes.

A nightly training job takes too long, so a developer raises the learning rate from 0.001 to 0.1. The job now stops after 9 epochs instead of 21, the pipeline stays green, and the change ships as a performance fix. A week later the model's error is clearly worse, and nobody links it to the "speed-up", because nothing failed. The job didn't get faster at reaching the same place. It gave up somewhere else.
Many developers treat the learning rate like a speed setting: turn it up and training finishes sooner with the same result. That's not a careless belief:

items.text: The name suggests it. A higher "rate" of learning sounds like learning the same thing faster.
Google's Machine Learning Crash Course itself describes the learning rate as a number that influences how quickly the model converges, and below a certain point that's exactly what you see.
Training cost really is the pain point. When a job takes hours, the knob with "rate" in its name is the first thing people reach for.

content.text: It's a half-truth. Raising a too-small learning rate does speed things up. But past a problem-dependent point, a bigger step stops changing

The learning rate scales every step

is that step's multiplier. The Crash Course's example: with a gradient of 2.5 and a learning rate of 0.01, the weight changes by 0.025. Multiply the learning rate by 100 and every step is 100 times longer, whether or not the minimum is that far away.

content.text: Google's Deep Learning Tuning Playbook puts it bluntly: any workload becomes unstable if the learning rate is too large.
What it looks like in code
Here's a linear model trained with stochastic gradient descent on scikit-learn's built-in diabetes dataset (442 patients, 10 measurements), with a constant learning rate (

tabs.label: ❌ Wrong
tabs.code:
from sklearn.datasets import load_diabetes
from sklearn.linear_model import SGDRegressor
from sklearn.metrics import mean_squared_error
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler

X, y = load_diabetes(return_X_y=True)
X = StandardScaler().fit_transform(X)

# "Training is slow: raise the learning rate so it finishes sooner"
for eta0 in [0.0001, 0.001, 0.1, 1.0]:
    sgd = SGDRegressor(learning_rate="constant", eta0=eta0, random_state=0)
    sgd.fit(X, y)  # no error, no warning, even when it diverges
    mse = mean_squared_error(y, sgd.predict(X))
    print(f"eta0={eta0:<6} epochs {sgd.n_iter_:<4} training MSE {mse:.4g}")
# eta0=0.0001 epochs 184  training MSE 2879
# eta0=0.001  epochs 21   training MSE 2879
# eta0=0.1    epochs 9    training MSE 4624
# eta0=1.0    epochs 6    training MSE 9.336e+25

tabs.label: ✅ Right
tabs.code:
from sklearn.datasets import load_diabetes
from sklearn.linear_model import LinearRegression, SGDRegressor
from sklearn.metrics import mean_squared_error
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler

X, y = load_diabetes(return_X_y=True)
X = StandardScaler().fit_transform(X)
exact = mean_squared_error(y, LinearRegression().fit(X, y).predict(X))
print(f"exact solution          training MSE {exact:.4g}")

# Sweep on a log scale; "adaptive" divides the step by 5 when loss stalls
for eta0 in [0.001, 0.01, 0.1, 1.0]:
    sgd = SGDRegressor(learning_rate="adaptive", eta0=eta0, random_state=0)
    sgd.fit(X, y)
    mse = mean_squared_error(y, sgd.predict(X))
    print(f"eta0={eta0:<6} epochs {sgd.n_iter_:<4} training MSE {mse:.4g}")
# exact solution          training MSE 2860
# eta0=0.001  epochs 803  training MSE 2874
# eta0=0.01   epochs 81   training MSE 2865
# eta0=0.1    epochs 87   training MSE 2860
# eta0=1.0    epochs 239  training MSE 2862

epochs in a row. With a big constant step, the weights keep jumping across the minimum, the loss stops improving, and the stopping rule fires. The run ended early because it got stuck bouncing, not because it arrived.

The best value depends on everything else

The Crash Course stresses that the ideal learning rate is problem-dependent, so there's no universal default to copy. It also moves when other settings change: the Tuning Playbook lists the learning rate among the hyperparameters that interact most with batch size, and says changing the batch size typically means tuning again from scratch. Feature scale matters too; the scikit-learn guide notes SGD is sensitive to it, which is why both scripts standardize first.

content.text: Try values a factor of 10 apart (0.0001, 0.001, 0.01, 0.1, 1), plot each run's loss curve, then refine around the best. The Tuning Playbook starts its instability diagnosis the same way: sweep, find the best learning rate, then look at the loss curves just above it.

How to apply it in your project
before any gradient-based model in a pipeline, so one learning rate suits every feature.
When you change the learning rate, compare the final training and validation loss. A run that stops sooner may simply have stopped improving.
Search on a log scale, pick the best region, then try a few values in between. Keep the sweep's loss curves in your experiment notes.
. In deep learning, the Playbook suggests a warmup, which ramps the learning rate up from 0, when training is unstable early on.
A new batch size, optimizer or feature set can move the best learning rate. Rerun the sweep instead of reusing an old value.

items.text: The learning rate multiplies every step; it changes where training goes, not just how fast.
Below the best value, raising it speeds training up; above it, the loss bounces or explodes.
Fewer epochs can mean the run stopped improving, not that it converged; compare final loss.
Find it with a log-scale sweep, use a schedule, and retune when batch size or features change.
